summaries.example: Imagine two children carrying a large box. If one child happens to walk toward the same place while the other carries the box, that is not really a shared task. But if they agree to carry it together, adjust their steps, and help each other, they are acting together. Their actions are connected by a shared plan.
summaries.summary: Shared agency is about what it means for people to do something together. Two people may perform similar actions by coincidence, like several people running to a shelter when it starts to rain. That does not automatically make their action shared. A dance group running to the same shelter as part of a performance is different because the movements belong to a joint activity. Philosophers debate what makes the difference. Some focus on a special kind of intention about what “we” are doing. Others try to explain shared action using each person’s ordinary plans, provided those plans fit together and include cooperation. The entry also examines how shared intentions begin, how people may be responsible to one another during a joint activity, and whether groups can sometimes be genuine thinking or acting subjects.
key_ideas: People can make similar movements without acting together. Shared action needs a meaningful connection between their aims and plans.
Some philosophers think shared action depends on special “we” intentions. Others explain it through ordinary individual intentions that are properly connected.
Participants may need to coordinate their plans, recognize one another’s roles, and be ready to cooperate.
Some philosophers think shared activities create responsibilities between participants, while others argue that these responsibilities are not always essential.
The entry also asks whether some groups can have a mind of their own, especially when a group makes rational decisions that do not match any one member’s view.
summaries.why_it_matters: We often depend on people acting together: teams, families, clubs, workplaces, and governments all make plans and decisions. Understanding shared agency helps us ask when a group has really acted, who is committed to what, and whether a rule or decision belongs to the group or was simply forced on its members. It also helps explain why cooperation is more than many separate actions happening nearby.

important_terms.definition: Agency is a person’s ability to choose and carry out actions.
Shared agency happens when people act together as part of a connected activity, rather than merely doing similar things by chance.
An intention is a plan or aim that guides what someone tries to do.
A participatory intention is a person’s commitment to taking part in something the group is doing.
A mutual obligation is a responsibility that participants owe to one another in a shared activity.

questions_to_think_about: If two people do the same thing at the same time, what would show that they are really acting together?
Can people share a goal if they have different reasons for joining?
When should someone be allowed to leave a group activity?
Can a team make a reasonable decision that no single team member believes?

summaries.example: Suppose representatives from two rival political parties help pass a law. They may support the law for incompatible reasons, and neither may accept the other’s broader political goals. Still, they can participate in a shared legislative activity if their intentions and plans are sufficiently coordinated. This suggests that shared agency may require cooperation and practical coordination without requiring identical motives or values.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates the nature of shared agency: the way individuals act together in joint activities. The basic challenge is to distinguish genuine collective action from a coincidence or sum of individual acts. The Intention Thesis proposes that each participant has a participatory intention connected to the joint activity. Philosophers disagree about whether these intentions are ordinary intentions arranged in a special interpersonal structure or a primitive kind of intention that cannot be reduced to individual agency. The discussion examines how intentions must interrelate, including coordination of subplans, mutual recognition, practical constraints, and possible agreement about how an activity begins or changes. A further problem arises from the fact that each participant should be committed to the whole activity, although the whole is not solely within that participant’s power to settle. The entry then considers directed obligations between participants and the possibility that certain groups, through rational decision procedures, possess minds of their own.
key_ideas: The central ontological problem is to explain what remains after the individual actions in a joint activity are distinguished from a mere aggregation of acts.

Searle treats participatory intention as a distinctive, non-reducible kind of individual intention. Tuomela, Miller, and Bratman instead develop accounts that seek to explain shared agency through appropriately related individual intentions.

Bratman emphasizes coordinated planning: participants’ subplans should be mutually satisfiable, and participants should be disposed to revise them when they conflict. The source also discusses whether this coordination can be reduced to ordinary norms of consistency and means-end coherence.

A difficulty for every account is that each person must be committed to the whole activity, even though no one person can settle what all participants will do. Proposed responses include conditional interdependent intentions, reasonable prediction of others’ intentions, intending one’s part, and team reasoning.

Gilbert argues that shared activity involves directed commitments or mutual obligations between participants. Bratman questions whether such obligations are essential, while other proposals weaken them or interpret them differently.

The group-mind debate concerns whether some collectives are genuine intentional subjects. Premise-driven decision procedures may produce rational group judgments that no individual member holds, but critics ask whether the group’s rationality can instead be explained by the members’ own intentions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Shared agency has consequences for ethics, law, politics, economics, psychology, and theories of knowledge. It affects how we understand cooperation, promises, testimony, collective responsibility, institutional decisions, and the status of laws or institutions created through common action. The debate also tests a broader philosophical question: can social phenomena be explained entirely from individual minds and actions, or do some forms of collective agency require genuinely interpersonal or group-level concepts?

important_terms.definition: Agency is the capacity to act intentionally and to guide conduct through practical reasoning.
Shared agency is agency exercised by multiple individuals in a coordinated, cooperative activity.
The Intention Thesis holds that shared activity involves a participatory intention in each participant that distinguishes acting together from a mere collection of individual acts.
A participatory intention is an individual’s intention concerning participation in a joint activity, such as intending that we perform an action or intending to do one’s part.
Practical intersubjectivity is the idea that each participant’s intentions and plans function as rational constraints on the others’ related intentions and plans.
A contralateral commitment is a directed commitment one participant has toward another participant in a shared activity.
The settling condition says that intention normally settles something the agent takes to be within the agent’s control.
A group mind is a group understood as a genuine subject of intentional attitudes, rather than merely a convenient summary of its members’ attitudes.

questions_to_think_about: Can ordinary individual intentions fully explain shared agency, or is a distinctive participatory intention required?
If two participants have the same goal but incompatible subplans, do they share an intention? Why?
Does a person’s commitment to a joint activity give another participant a claim against that person?
How can someone intend that a group act when the group’s action is not entirely under that person’s control?
When does a group’s rational decision justify treating it as more than a summary of individual decisions?

summaries.example: A student newspaper team plans an issue about school activities. One student interviews athletes, another designs the pages, and a third checks facts. Their work counts as a shared activity only if their plans fit together and each treats the others’ work as part of the project. If two students secretly plan opposite layouts and never intend to cooperate, the similar goal of making a newspaper is not enough.
summaries.summary: Shared agency asks what makes an activity something that people do together. The entry contrasts genuine joint action with cases in which individuals happen to perform similar actions, such as people independently running for shelter in a storm. A major proposal, the Intention Thesis, says that each participant has a participatory intention connected to the shared activity. Philosophers disagree about how to understand this intention. Some accounts reduce it to ordinary personal intentions that include doing one’s part and coordinating with others. Critics argue that such conditions might describe people whose actions merely produce a common result without real cooperation. Other accounts treat participatory intention as a special, basic form of intention. The entry then examines how participants’ intentions must fit together, how they can form or revise a joint commitment, and whether shared activity creates mutual obligations. Finally, it considers the possibility that some groups have minds of their own when their decision procedures generate rational conclusions not held by individual members.
key_ideas: Shared action is not just a pile of separate actions. People must be connected by intentions, plans, or other conditions that make the activity cooperative.
One disagreement concerns whether a shared intention is a special basic kind of intention or a structure built from ordinary intentions held by individuals.
A plan to do something together is not enough if participants’ subplans conflict. For example, painting one wall green and purple all over cannot both happen as planned.

Some philosophers say participants must treat one another’s plans as reasons that matter when they plan their own actions. Others say people can share an activity even when their personal reasons differ.
The entry discusses whether starting, changing, or ending a shared activity requires everyone’s agreement. It also considers whether participants owe one another performance of their parts.
Some theorists argue that certain groups can be genuine agents when their decision process produces rational judgments that cannot be explained simply by adding up members’ opinions.
summaries.why_it_matters: People constantly act in groups, from school projects and sports teams to political institutions. The idea of shared agency helps us understand what cooperation really involves and why a group decision may have a different status from many private decisions. It also raises practical questions about responsibility, permission to withdraw, obligations to teammates, and whether institutions can act in ways that are not reducible to what any one member thinks.

important_terms.definition: Agency means being able to direct one’s actions through choices, plans, and reasons.
Shared agency is when people take part in one connected activity and coordinate their actions, rather than simply acting at the same time.
An intention is a plan or commitment about what someone will do.
A participatory intention is an individual intention about joining in a group activity, such as intending that we complete a task.
A reductive account explains shared agency using resources that already explain individual agency, such as separate personal intentions.
Practical intersubjectivity means that the plans and intentions of one participant place rational constraints on the plans and intentions of the others.
A mutual obligation is a responsibility that participants may have toward one another within a shared activity.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between cooperating and merely doing similar things?
Can a group activity work when members have different reasons for participating?
Should one person be able to quit a shared project without consulting the others?
Is it fair to hold someone responsible for a group plan they did not personally support?
Could a team’s decision be rational even if every member would choose something else on their own?
